"A secret session of the House of Commons was held at 3 o'clock p.m. on Tuesday the 24th February, 1942.
"The sitting was devoted to the question of the defence of Canada in its widest qualification. Statements were made by the Honourable Messrs. Ralston, Power and Macdonald, the ministers in charge of National Defence. A variety of questions dealing with different aspects of the war were asked and answered. Many details were given the members of the house.
J. Allison Glen,
Speaker."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROTECTED AREAS-JAPANESE NATIONALS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MEASURES FOR SECURITY
speechtext:
I wish to lay on the table a copy of an order in council which was passed yesterday amending the defence of Canada regulations and giving the Minister of Justice increased powers to require persons to leave "protected areas." It might be of service to the house if I were to table at this time a number of orders in council that have been passed which have a special relation to conditions as they exist in the province of British Columbia as a result of situations arising out of Japan's declaration of war.
The order in council which I have just tabled, P.C. 14S6, amends the defence of Canada regulations so as to provide authority for the Minister of Justice to require any or all persons to leave a protected area as defined by order of the Minister of National Defence 44561-52
and to impose restrictions in respect of their employment, business, movement or places of residence. Under this authority the Minister of Justice may also prohibit or restrict the possession or use by any or all persons in the protected area of any specified articles and require their delivery to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In short, the defence of Canada regulations as now amended give the Minister of Justice full power to take any required security measures with regard to any person if in the protected area. The protected area in British Columbia has already been defined by the Minister of National Defence as the coastal area between the Cascade mountains and the sea, including all the islands off the coast of British Columbia.
In addition to the above mentioned order in council, the following orders have previously been passed relating to security on the Pacific coast:
P.C. 9591, December 7, 1941 and P.C. 9760, December 16, 1941, respecting compulsory registration of all persons of Japanese race. That has already been tabled.
P.C. 9761, December 16, 1941, providing for control of vessels used or operated by persons of Japanese race.
P.C. 251 of January 13, 1942, prohibiting the issuance of fishing licences to persons of Japanese race, and prohibiting such persons from serving on fishing vessels. That has also been tabled.
P.C. 365, January 16, 1942, amending the Defence of Canada regulations so as to authorize the Minister of National Defence, with the concurrence of the Minister of Justice to declare any area in Canada a protected area, or if it appears necessary or expedient so to do, and in the public interest, and in respect of such areas conferring certain powers with regard to the persons and property of any enemy aliens.
P.C. 1271, February 17, 1942, providing for the establishment of a Canadian-Japanese corf struction corps, to be formed by Canadian nationals of Japanese racial origin, and establishing conditions of enrolment and terms of service for the said corps.
P.C. 1348, February 19, 1942, authorizing the establishment of work camps for male enemy aliens including Japanese nationals, on projects outside protected areas.
P.C. 1365 of February 19, 1942, prohibiting the possession of fire-arms or explosives by persons of Japanese race.
P.C. 1457 of February 24, 1942, regulating the acquisition of land or any interest therein, or the growing of crops in Canada by persons of Japanese race and by Japanese controlled companies.

Japanese Nationals

Perhaps I
should give to the house a statement I gave to the press this morning. I would have made it to the house first but I thought it was in the interest of law and order out on

the Pacific coast that this communication should reach British Columbia without delay.
The statement was to the effect that power had been given to the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) to exclude any or all persons, regardless of their citizenship, from protected areas as defined under the defence of Canada regulations.
The new regulation corresponds very closely to the proclamation issued by the President of the United States on Friday.
Under the amended order the Minister of Justice may require any or all persons, whether British subjects or not, to leave a protected area. He is further authorized to impose such restrictions as he may specify in respect of their employment, business, movements or places of residence. He can prohibit or restrict the possession or use by any or all persons in the protected area of any specified articles and can require the delivery of such articles to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In short, the defence of Canada regulations as now amended give the Minister of Justice full power to take any required security measure within the protected area with regard to any person within that area.
The protected area in British Columbia in which the new order will apply has been defined by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) as the coastal belt between the Cascade mountains and the sea, including all the islands off the coast of British Columbia.
It is the policy of the government to use the powers of tlhis order to take all necessary security measures to safeguard the defences of the Pacific coast of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SERVICE BETWEEN ISLAND AND MAINLAND
speechtext:
I desire to call the attention of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Transport, who I am sorry is not in his seat, to the situation which has arisen in connection with the car ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I ask the house to bear with me while I give a brief recital of the present position as I see it.
On the 23rd instant, the day before yesterday, the ferry Prince Edward Island was held up at Borden with a leaky boiler, and there is now no conveyance by boat between the mainland and the island. All freight and passenger movement are held up, and the only chance to get on and off the island is by air. Just how long it will take to repair the boiler is not known. I am advised that last week there were over one hundred1 carloads of freight at Tormentine awaiting shipment to the island, and in addition to the ordinary shipments of live stock moving off the island, over two hundred reefer cars were required to ship potatoes to the United States. These potatoes represent a value to the farmers of approximately $1,000 per car, and if the situation does not improve very shortly a very severe loss will be sustained. I understand that the transportation committee of the Charlottetown board of trade met on the 23rd instant and passed a resolution, which was telegraphed to the Prime Minister, but so far as I know no answer has yet been received.

I placed some questions about this matter on the order paper for the purpose of eliciting some information, but the answers brought down on Monday last indicate that nothing is being done to improve the situation. Of course, when these questions were placed on the order paper the present ferry was not out of commission. I am also advised that if an. order had been given in the United States for a new ferry within a reasonable time after the Charlottetown was lost, that order could have been filled, since they are filling orders over there for icebreakers and so on for the great lakes.	.
Will the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Transport, or in his absence the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who has had perhaps more to do with this matter than anyone else, indicate what is intended to be done to cope with the present situation, which is rapidly going from bad to worse, perhaps through no fault on the part of anyone in particular but because of delay in dealing with the situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SERVICE BETWEEN ISLAND AND MAINLAND
speechtext:
This matter has been giving
the government a great deal of concern. I assume that the Department of Munitions and Supply is the bottleneck. The position is that in order to rebuild this ferry we would have to give up a berth in one of our shipyards for a period of some fifteen months. We would have to divert sufficient steel to build probably two or three twin screw corvettes, which are badly needed; and considering the urgency of our naval requirements and of shipbuilding generally, we have not thought it advisable to do this.
My hon. friend is quite mistaken as to the possibility of having the ferry built in the United States. That possibility was explored immediately after the sinking. We scoured the second-hand market there, and looked into the position of the shipyards. At that time every shipyard was controlled by the government, and it was quite impossible to get a berth.
The service is carried on at the moment 'by a car ferry which handled the service until 1929, I think, and which is a perfectly good ferry. There are two car ferries on the run, but at present only one operates; and it is not unusual for the present ferry to carry on the service for six weeks or two months at this time of year. That ferry is operating. There was a short delay while a boiler was overhauled or repaired, but these things do occur when there is only one boat in operation, causing a temporary tie-up of cars. But unless this service 'has changed tremendously

Armed Forces-Farmers' Sons
since earlier years the present car ferry should be able to handle the traffic with reasonable satisfaction to the people on the island. At this time of year, when the floe ice is heavy, the service always has been subject to short interruptions. It is not unusual to have a ferry go out to sea and be away for thirty-six hours before being able to dock on the other side; at least that lias occurred more than once. In the meantime I would remind -hon. members that a second service has been inaugurated between Wood island and Pictou, which I believe will relieve toe situation considerably during the summer months.
I can assure every hon. member that the government is exceedingly anxious to rectify this situation, but at the moment that could be done only at great cost to our war effort. We are organized in one set of yards to build cargo boats, which we are launching every two months from every berth. It would .perhaps mean losing eight or ten cargo vessels if we built a new ferry or, alternatively, losing two or three corvettes. In this period of war we must weigh the relative urgency of the needs in both directions, and that we have . been doing. The moment we think we can spare a berth of any sort -that can build a successor to the Charlottetown, toe boat will be built. In the meantime a ferry has been found, I think in San Francisco or Los Angeles, which -may be of some service as a stand-by boat. This is being examined very closely, and if it is found at all satisfactory it will be brought around and put on the service for such assistance as it is able to render.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE

speechtext:
Hon.' N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, respecting the taking of a plebiscite in every electoral district in Canada and the taking of the votes of such plebiscite of Canadian service voters stationed within and without Canada.
Right .Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	The bill which is now
before the house for its second reading is, as the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), who introduced it, announced a few days ago, in the nature of a general plebiscite act; that is to say, it makes provision for the taking of a plebiscite which ordinarily would be as applicable to a 'plebiscite on one subject as another. The intention, however, is that the bill should be for one plebiscite only, and that the plebiscite when taken, shall have reference to only one question. That question has already been made clear to the members of the house and the public, but I will take occasion at once to bring again to the attention of the house its exact wording.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
It will be recalled that in the speech from the throne it was announced, as part of government policy, that a plebiscite would be taken on the question of removing a certain limitation which now is imposed upon the government with respect to the enlistment of men for service overseas. The question which it is intended to ask the public in the plebiscite is the following:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
As I said, at the time of speaking on the address, the question is very simple in its language and meaning and is a straightforward one. I do not think it is capable of any more than one interpretation. It asks the people of Canada whether they are willing to release the government from a certain limitation which arises out of past commitments with respect to the enlistment of men for overseas. If the answer is in the affirmative it will mean that the government, according to the opinion expressed by the people, has been released from commitments that have been made; if it is in the negative it will mean that the majority of the electors are of the opinion that the government should continue to be governed by the commitment that was made at the time of the last general election and on previous occasions, and on subsequent occasions as well.
The subject of the plebiscite has been debated at such length that it would perhaps seem unnecessary to discuss it further. My purpose this afternoon is not so much to attempt to add to what has been said but rather, if possible, to clear away some of the confusion that has arisen out of the discussion that has already taken place.
To that end, let me first of all make quite clear the purpose of the plebiscite. As I have said, the purpose is to give the government- I put it in general terms-a perfectly free hand to deal with all matters affecting the war in the manner which, in its judgment, is most in the national interest.
There is a distinction to be made between the legal powers which the government has and the moral authority which it possesses. With respect to the legal power, there can be no question whatever that this parliament has full power to do whatever it may decide to do with respect to the management of matters pertaining to the war. The one limitation which exists on that power so far as this parliament is concerned is not a legal limitation but a moral obligation.
There may be some who take the view that, in matters of government, in time of war, moral obligations count for nothing. May I
say that, in my opinion, moral obligations, especially where they relate to a specific measure, a concrete matter related to the war on which the government of the country itself has given a pledge, are as binding as any obligation could possibly be. To say that the parliament of Canada, which derives its powers from the people, after a solemn pledge has been given to the people on a matter which is of deep concern to them, is released from this pledge the moment the people have elected it, is simply for parliament itself to create a precedent which would be subversive of parliamentary institutions.
Let me ask first of all how this limitation arose. It arose out of a situation that existed several years ago in this country. That of itself is significant as indicating how long the public memory is with respect to matters which affect the people themselves. I would pause here to say that the public memory is going to be long in the matter of how this parliament views its moral obligations as well as its legal powers. It is because I feel very strongly that the people of Canada will wish to have their present and their future governments pay the utmost regard to pledges given to the electorate that I feel it all important that this matter of past commitments should be presented to the people in the form of a question which will secure their opinion, before the time comes when the government may be called upon to consider whether further action than it is empowered now to take, should or should not become necessary later on.
During the last war the question of conscription came up near the end of the conflict. I will not go into what took place at the time except to remind hon. members of the fact that nothing in the political history of Canada since Confederation has given rise to so much bitterness, so much ill feeling, or has done so much in the way of dividing the peoples of this country, setting one lot against another, as did the conscription issue at that particular time, and the manner in which it was dealt with by the government of the day. Now it was because of that fact that, when the government of the day saw looming on the horizon the possibility of a future war, it was recognized that this question of conscription would present itself immediately. It was of importance therefore to national unity that a position should be taken and stated by the administration which would prevent any of the kind of controversy and bitterness which had previously arisen, and would maintain the unity of the country at a time when the situation might be most critical. Having that in mind, the government of the day-this was before the present war began-and, not merely

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
the government, but members of the opposition and members of all parties in this House of Commons, expressed very frankly and emphatically on the floor of this parliament their view that, if another war came, and it became necessary to consider the sending of men overseas to participate in what was then thought might be a war confined to Europe alone, the only method that would be resorted to for overseas would be the one of voluntary enlistment-there would be no compulsion, no conscription. I think I am right when I say that that was the view which was generally expressed before the war by all parties in this house. It was expressed for the one reason that it was felt that it was absolutely necessary to maintain, as far as that might be possible, the unity of the country at a time when it might be faced with the great crisis of war.
But let me go a step further. When the war came in Europe and this parliament met to decide whether Canada would enter the war or not, a declaration was made by the government of the day that, if Canada did enter the war, there would not be compulsory service for overseas, but that service for overseas would be by voluntary enlistment. That declaration was made when this house was deciding whether Canada should go into the war or not. And that statement was made not by the government to hon. members of parliament only but by members of parliament of all parties speaking to the people of the country, and assuring them of the position that would be taken. I submit that no more solemn undertaking could possibly have been given to the people of Canada than that which was given to them by their representatives in the House of Commons at that time.
What was the effect of giving that declaration? The effect was that, when Canada decided to go into the war, this House of Commons, I think to a man-there may have been an exception, but practically to a man -decided that Canada should participate in the war at Britain's side. We were told beforehand that it was all nonsense to ask parliament to decide whether the country should ,go into the war, we were told-I am speaking now of what the government was told by its opponents-that the government should decide that question; not leave it to the people's representatives in parliament to decide what they should do. I took the position very strongly at the time that parliament would decide, and I suppose no one received more abuse and criticism from certain sections of the press and public speakers than I did for taking that stand; I took the position that Canada would not go automatically into war (Mr. Mackenzie King.]
just because one part of the empire might be at war, but that we would decide on the merits of the case as the situation was known, and would take our own action by the vote of the people's representatives in parliament.
Having given the assurance that conscription would not be resorted to in connection with enlistment for service overseas, this parliament voted practically unanimously to enter the war. But that was not the only occasion on which the position was asserted.
WTe also had a general election in 1940 to decide what administration was to carry on the affairs of the country during the period of war. At that time from one end of Canada to the other members of the government renewed to the people of Canada the undertaking which I have just cited, as the one which would be followed in time of war. Hon. members opposite have been referring to this pledge or commitment as "Mr. King's commitment", "to relieve Mr. King of his commitment", "relieve the Prime Minister of his commitment". May I say that the commitment was not a commitment of myself alone. To begin with, it was a commitment on the part of all my colleagues in the government, it had been made in this House of Commons in the presence of every one of them; it was a commitment made in the name of the entire party which supports the administration; and, may I say, a commitment quite as broad, quite as emphatic, was made by the leader of the opposition of that day on behalf of the Conservative party in this house. The very same commitment was made on behalf of the Conservative party of Canada in this House of Commons by its then leader, it was made also on the platforms of this country by its leader in terms just as emphatic as anyone on this side of the house could have made it.
So that there will be no misunderstanding of this, let me give hon. members exactly what the then leader of the Conservative party, and of the official opposition, Doctor Manion said, speaking in this House of Commons on March 30, 1939; as reported in Hansard at page 2440:
In the last war the conscription of men to go to the front caused violent racial antagonisms, much disharmony, bitterness and misunderstanding-conditions from which as yet we have not wholly recovered, and on top of that I believe I am expressing the opinion of authorities when I say that it was of no real military value so far as the empire was concerned.
He stated that as far as he could ascertain only some ten thousand men at the most got into the fighting line as a result of conscription. Then he went on to say:
The policy that I suggest is the one which I gave three days ago in an interview: first.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
that there should be no conscription of Canadians to serve outside the borders of Canada; second, that we should have full cooperation with the British empire short of the conscription of men to serve outside our borders.
That was the statement Doctor Manion as leader of the official opposition, and of the Conservative party, made to parliament. But he also made similar statements on the public platforms during the campaign of 1940. Here is what Doctor Manion said at Quebec, speaking in the name of his party:
I stated on March 30, 1939, just about a year ago, in the House of Commons, that I was opposed to conscription because of its failure in the last war, and because it had stirred up misunderstanding and strife in our country, when the duty of our public men is to hold this country together, rather than to break it up. I have not waited until I came to the province of Quebec to make this statement. I made it a month ago at Brockville in the opening speech of my campaign. I have made it more than twenty times, since then, in almost every speech which I have delivered as far west as Victoria, B.C. Thus I have set forth my attitude in five provinces of Canada before coming to Quebec, and I state here again to-night that I am against conscription and that a national government such as I propose will not put in conscription.
Now there is the statement made by the leader of the Conservative party who was asking the country to support his party-not, it is true, under its old name of the Conservative party, but under the new name which it was taking for the purpose of the election -national government party-a pledge that if a national government party were returned they would not put conscription into force.
Now let me assume for a moment that a national government party had been returned. I ask my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, if he had been a member of that government, or Doctor Manion's successor in that government, whether he would have felt that he had no obligation whatever to see that that particular undertaking was lived up to? Would he have taken the position that although he had been returned to power on a specific pledge solemnly given to the people in the different provinces at a time of war, in a general election when they were being asked to return his administration rather than another, that having been returned to this parliament would he then immediately thereafter have turned around and said, "I recognize no obligation in this matter to those who elected the administration, I am going to proceed without any reference to the people at all?" I do not believe my hon. friend would have done that, and I am surprised that he criticizes me for wishing to have the people pass on this question in order that the government may be freed of all
limitations upon its authority to act, except its responsibility to parliament, and through parliament to the people.
It is true that my hon. friend has said to me, "I think what you should have done was come to the House of Commons and ask the house to release you, and I am sure the house would have done so readily." But may I say to my hon. friend that my undertaking in this matter, as Prime Minister of the country, was not given to this House of Commons; it was given to the people of Canada. It was given, just as the pledge of his leader of that day was given, not to the House of Commons but to the people. It is true that a statement to the same effect was made to the house before the recent general elections, and before the war, but it was not a statement to the members of the house so much as a statement of what we and our parties and followers would do if we were faced with a situation which demanded the question being decided one way or the other. The pledge was given later direct to the people, to the electorate themselves; it was a pledge made between the leaders of two great political parties in Canada and the electorate of this country in regard to the most solemn question that could have been put before them at that particular time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I see it either we are going to destroy the faith of the people of Canada in their public men and in the responsibility of parliament to the people themselves, if we ignore these pledges, or we are going to maintain that faith by making it perfectly clear to the people that we regard such power as we have as coming from the people themselves and that we intend to be ever mindful of this, and that if we have given a solemn pledge to them we intend to carry out that pledge. If, after situations have arisen which did not exist at the time a pledge was made, we believe in their own interests we should be released from that pledge and we take the necessary steps to that end, by consulting the people first, then I say we are helping to keep the faith of the people in their public men and in their parliament.
That is why to my mind this question is fundamental. It goes to the very roots of government itself, the very source from which power is derived by a parliament. Has my hon. friend any authority other than that which comes from the people? Have I any power except that which comes from the people? Is that power changed the moment I get into parliament? Being returned by the votes of the people themselves, I have constantly to keep in mind, as I think every
826	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
member of parliament must, that obligation, which is an abiding obligation with respect to membership in any House of Commons worthy of the name.
Well, now, that being the purpose of the plebiscite, let me state the present position. The position is that the government has full power with respect to everything, excepting one thing; and that one thing is that commitment, that obligation, with respect to the enlisting of men for overseas service. There the government is not free. You may ask why the government should come forward at the present time and ask to be made free. First of all may I make it clear that it is not because of any situation that exists at the moment. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has made it perfectly clear that with respect to voluntary enlistment we are obtaining men for overseas service at the present time as rapidly as we can train them. For our programme this year, and up to March, 1943, there is an honest belief on the part of the government that we will be able to get the men by voluntary enlistment for service overseas, and will not have to resort to conscription. But no one can say how long this war is going to last. No one can say what particular turn it is going to take. None of us knows what the conditions are going to be a few months hence, or several months hence, or a year or two hence. What we all know is this, that every month of this war has made it apparent to every member of this House of Commons, and I think should have made it apparent to every citizen of Canada, that a government cannot possess too much in the way of freedom to take the course that may be demanded in the national interest at a time like the present. It is because of this we want to have perfect freedom of action as an administration, to have all the right to do what is in the public interest at the time the situation may demand it, and we feel we ought to be given this freedom as quickly as possible. The reason we want it, as I have stated already, is to be free to act in the manner which will best serve the interests of the people of Canada; the manner that will make Canada's wTar effort the most effective. That is the sole reason, and that is all that is involved in this plebiscite. Hon. members have been talking about conscription, about no conscription and the like. That is not the issue in this plebiscite. This is the issue: Is the government of Canada, in time of war, to have freedom to take whatever action it thinks most advisable with respect to the furtherance of Canada's war effort?
That is the only question, and I am amazed that any person who has to do with the 
moulding of public opinion in Canada, with the making of its laws or who has to do with any political institution, could for a moment hesitate to give immediate support to a request of the kind. What argument can be urged against giving to a ministry the right to have full power in time of war to deal with any question, just as in time of peace it has full power to deal with any question that may come before it?
But there is another point I wish to bring out in connection with the special need for the plebiscite at this time, and it is this. First of all, the government is being put in an entirely wrong position before the people of this country and before the world just because we have not that full power. I ask hon. members to reflect upon that. I have said that the public has a long memory. Other countries, other nations have memories as well. To-day we are in a great partnership with a large number of nations, who are helping us as we are helping them. It is important that our position should be perfectly clear. It is being represented to the people of this country, and it is being represented to the people of Britain, the people of the United States and the people of all the allied nations, that this government is not seeking to have an all out war effort. Why? Because it is precluded, under a commitment which it has given and to which it is adhering, from resorting to conscription for men for service overseas. In other words the all out war effort is being identified with that one single thing, namely the commitment against having conscription for overseas service whether that should ever become necessary or not.
That is putting the government in an entirely false position. Let us take the position as it is to-day. Would anyone say that we have not been working as hard as we possibly could toward a full out war effort? Will anyone say that at the present time, if we had that full power, we would be resorting to conscription for overseas service? No one will say that, because it is not necessary, has not become necessary, and may never become necessary. Nevertheless as long as that commitment is there we are being represented to the people of our own and other countries as a government unwilling to go the lengths other countries are willing to go, even should necessity for so doing become clearly manifest. That is a false position and a very wrong one in which to have the government placed.
Moreover, the present position in regard to that one commitment places the parliament of Canada, as well, in a false position. Suppose the question of conscription were urgent at this time, and we wished to discuss it on the

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
floor of the house, could we have a free discussion of conscription on its merits, with that commitment binding many hon. members at the present time? The very minute the subject were brought up, one hon. member after another, if it suited his purpose, would rise in his place in the house and say, "I cannot discuss this question, because the government is committed not even to raise it." So long as that commitment is there, no matter how the war may develop, there can be no discussion of the merits of the question of compulsory service for overseas. I say that that is putting parliament in a wrong position before the people of Canada.
I have not any fear, personally, that parliament will not take the right course with respect to any phase of the war effort, once it is debated on its merits. I have faith in the judgment of the House of Commons to do what is the wisest and the right thing, having respect to the merits of the case. But in existing circumstances I do not want to see this parliament placed longer in a position where it cannot even discuss the merits of an all-important question with regard to Canada's war effort. And so I say to those who are taking exception to the course which the government is pursuing that they are only helping to place their own parliament in a position in which no parliament should be placed in a time of war.
I would say further, that not only is it putting the government in a false position to have its hands tied at this time, in the manner indicated, and that it is putting parliament in a false position, but it is also putting Canada in a false position, before all countries of the world, including her allies in the war.
We have seen in communciations which have appeared from time to time, and we have heard in the public addresses, what has been said recently about the position of the United States vis-a-vis Canada. Notwithstanding the fact that for over two years Canada has been sending thousands of men across the seas, we have in the last month or two heard it said that Canada's war effort is not as fine as that of the United States, and why, forsooth, not that they have sent large numbers of men overseas, not that the United States have thousands of men, men who have been in the war for two years, but solely because there are alleged limitations on our war effort since we are not able to send a man overseas under compulsion, regardless of the fact that up to the present we have been and may continue to be able to get all we require under the voluntary system.
I do not believe Canada should be placed in that false position. We should not be placed in that position before the United States. We should not be placed in that false position
before Great Britain and, not only before our allies, but also before the enemy. It must be remembered that, as some are only too anxious to do in this country, the enemy will construe this commitment as a limitation on the war effort of Canada.
I say on these grounds, Mr. Speaker, I feel very strongly the time has come when that limitation should be removed, and when the government should be given the utmost freedom to deal with any phase of the war effort as it thinks best subject always to its responsibility to parliament.
I have said that this is not a question of conscription. Hon. members opposite have been saying, "Why do you not have a referendum, and refer the question of conscription itself to the people?"

speechtext:
And that is w'here I entirely disagree with my hon. friend. If it was not an issue it was because the leaders of all parties took similar positions, and the position so adopted was that there would be no question of conscription. But that makes the obligation all the greater on every hon. member sitting in the house to see that, before that question is so much as discussed, he should be released from any commitment which may have been made.
In reference to whether the plebiscite is to be in reality a referendum, there is a question which is being asked now which changes the plebiscite into a referendum- and I believe my hon. friend asked this question only a day or two ago-it is, "What are you going to do if the decision is such-and-such?" He wishes me to say that I am going to do so-and-so. If I were to give him an undertaking at this time, and that undertaking is before the people when the question is put before them, is that not a referendum? That is, I commit myself to one course or to the other, and the people then are being asked to decide whether the government should take it or not. In other words I throw on the people of this country the onus of making a political and military decision, when the only body by which such decision should be taken on a question of this kind is the government which is responsible for such decision, advised by its military advisers, and taking all other relevant facts into consideration and debating its decisions on the floor of parliament, thereby making itself responsible to parliament for the decisions it makes.
[DOT]"Mr. Mackenzie King.]
That brings me to the question of evading responsibility. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) used some language the other day to which I thought I might raise objection when he spoke. I decided, however, to refer to it later on. He described as a subterfuge the course the government is taking. I believe the term "subterfuge" as applied to government policy in a matter of this kind is one which you, Mr. Speaker, might properly have ruled out of order.
He also said the government lacked courage, and stated later in his remarks that the course we were adopting was an evasive one. Let us see how far it has been evasive. What are we doing in the matter of responsible government? With respect to responsible government, at the present time we have not full powers. Our powers are limited. We cannot have fully responsible government until there are no limitations upon our powers. What we are asking the people in this plebiscite is to give us perfect freedom, to give us full responsibility. We are not asking the people to relieve us of responsibility, we are not asking the people to make a decision for us, we are asking them to give us full responsibility. We will take it and we will exercise it in the light of our responsibility to their representatives in the House of Commons. Where is the evasion of responsible government in that?
Let me go back to the course my hon. friends propose to adopt, if I understand them aright. They say, "ignore the people; we are here now, we will decide this thing in this House of Commons without reference to the people at all". Well, I say that that is irresponsible government. Because we are here with a mandate which the people have given us, which is full in all particulars but one. They say with regard to that one particular, "we will ignore it altogether, we will pay no attention to it one way or another". Talk about being courageous, I do not see anything courageous about that. Courage comes when you face the people, not when you run away from them. That runaway course is the one my hon. friends opposite have been advocating right along.
WThen this government decided during the course of the war that it was going to hold to the constitution of this country by appealing to the people before the end of a five-year term to elect a new House of Commons, we were told we were doing the wrong thing, that we ought to stay here, that we ought to extend our term and theirs as members at tl- same time. "Don't face the people, that is wrong." I think the people showed that they were not ready to give much support to those who were not prepared to trust them

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
but who wanted to have power without recognizing the source from which political power comes. I hope I have made it clear that the government is not seeking to evade any responsibility. It wants full responsibility. When it has that responsibility, it will come here, not sheltering behind commitments, but with full authority to inform this house of the course it feels should be taken. It will stand or fall by the decision which it makes.
My hon. friend has said that the taking of this plebiscite means that it will delay matters in a time of war. What is it going to delay? Is it going to delay the production of munitions or equipment of war, or of ships? Is it going to delay the sending of airmen overseas? Is it going to delay the enlistment of men in the navy? Is it going to delay the enlistment of men in the army, either for service in Canada or overseas? I say it is not, not by one minute. More men are offering themselves for training to-day than the administration is able to train, and that will be so for some time to come. Is it delaying the production of food? Is it delaying contributions to the war loan? Some people recently said they ought to cut out contributions altogether because the government was seeking to recognize its obligations to the people. There is no delay anywhere. But there is a pause sufficiently long to allow the people to express their own views with respect to the future freedom of action that the government of this country should have the right to take.
Something has been said about the cost. I assume that it will cost sometlhing to take the plebiscite and I regret that it will be as long as it will 'be before the vote itself can be taken. But we are spending a good many billions of dollars at the present time and those billions of dollars are coming from the people. When this house undertakes to put through estimates amounting to something like three billion dollars in a year, I think the people of this country will be relieved to know that the government submitting those estimates -wants to be perfectly sure of their confidence in everything that it does; that it is prepared to trust them by going before them for increased powers when it feels that these increased powers are necessary in the public interest. I do not think that the plebiscite should cost very much. I believe that many of those who will serve as enumerators or *who will .perform other duties in connection with the taking of the plebiscite will be patriotic enough to realize that in this time of war this is one method whereby they can render a war service that will be a real contribution to the country at the present time. I should be surprised if many of them do not return to the public treasury the small amounts
that will be paid to them for the discharge of their important duties. I do not think the additional amount that will be required will be very great.
The taking of this plebiscite will not be using up war materials except .perhaps the paper that will be necessary for the instructions, the ballots and the like. That is the only material that I can see that is going to be used. Such other incidental expenses as may be necessary will I hope be met to a considerable extent in the way I have indicated. May I say that I feel very strongly that as this expense is one which the government is asking the people to incur at this time in the people's own interest, the people themselves will be quite willing that it should be incurred.
The last day upon which we discussed this question my hon. friend said that he was going to ask his party to vote "yes" on the plebiscite, that he was going to ask the country to vote "yes." Why did he not do that during the debate on the address? Why did he not come out when we were debating the address and say that he thought that every good Conservative in this country ought to support the government's proposal for a plebiscite? There is only one reason I can think of, and that is the one that was in the minds of newspaper editors, public speakers and others who came out so violently against the suggestion made in the speech from the throne. Four by-elections were due in this country and these patriotic gentlemen were going to have an issue at all costs. They were going to make an issue of something that had created all sorts of division in this country before. They were going to do this notwithstanding that it was war time and notwithstanding the fact that this government needed the services of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Labour perhaps as they had never been needed before since the war commenced. They were prepared to create this issue, they were determined to have these by-elections carried on in the manner of elections of past years when the question of conscription was the most controversial thing which had been raised in the history of Canada.
Where it suited them in Welland, and where they thought it was going to suit them in Toronto, the ground was put forward that the people were for conscription but that the present administration was opposed to conscription. Their candidate came out for conscription first and foremost. If we are going to judge from what took place, it is pretty clear that so far as Welland and Toronto are concerned, the people were in favour of the plebiscite.

There was no vote in Toronto.
830	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
t Mr. MACKENZIE KING: York South. The vote may not have been in Toronto, but most of the ammunition came from there. Quite the opposite campaign was waged against the government in another province in Canada. I have no complaint to make about the results. I think that so far as they signify anything with reference to the plebiscite itself, it is that so far as it has been possible for the people to speak on this matter we have had an expression favourable to our consulting them on this particular question.
During these campaigns every effort was made to becloud the war record of the government. That is one of the reasons this issue was raised. In every possible way it was sought to confuse the public mind rather than to clear it with respect to the issues themselves and with respect to the government's record in prosecuting the war. As I have said, the outcome has shown already the unwisdom of the course which was followed, by the government's opponents, the unwisdom of those tactics and the wisdom of the course which the government itself is taking at this time.
My hon. friend the other day asked me a number of questions with respect to the plebiscite. He said that he would like to know before the question was put to the people w'hat the government was going to do in certain eventualities. Let me answer the question first of all in a broad way. The government is asking the people for a free hand in order that it may do in the circumstances as they ma3' arise what is most in the interests of the people of Canada. We wish to make Canada's war effort as effective as it can possibly be made. What we shall do at any particular time will depend upon the course which we think at that time is necessary and advisable and most effective in Canada's war effort. That decision is not going to be made in the light of any one factor. It is going to be made in the light of all conditions as they exist and as they are known to the government at the time that it has to assume responsibility for any policy or any change of policy which it may deem advisable. Surely that is the only right position for an administration to have or to take.
My hon. friend says: Will you tell us, first of all, if the plebiscite is decided in the affirmative by a large majority, what you are doing to do? Then he asks: If it is decided by a very small majority, what are you going to do? Then next: If it is decided by say only thirty-seven per cent in favour, and the rest against, what are you going to do? Then I think his next query was: If several provinces are in favour, and one or two others are not in favour, what are you going to do? I 
think he had one other question: Yes, it was, if the vote is indecisive, what are you going to do?
Why did he not go on and ask several other questions? Why did he confine himself to thirty-seven per cent? Why did he not ask what we would do if only twenty-seven per cent or thirty-eight or thirty-nine per cent was in favour?
He submits to me a sort of political catechism and expects me to give an answer to every hypothetical question he can imagine. Why did he not ask: What are you going to do if the United States take such and such a course? Why did he not ask several other hypothetical questions? He asked enough to reveal his intention to embarrass the government, but I can assure him that he has not embarrassed me nor the administration in the least. The government will do in this matter as it has done, and as he himself would be doing to-day if he were in office. He would be saying this same thing to me if asked a similar question. The government will make its policy known at the time when it is essential to have it made known-and not before. All government policies should be made known at the right and proper time. This is not the right or the proper time to make any pronouncement as to what the government is going to do as a result of this vote, other than the pronouncement which I have already made, and made very clearly, that the government is going to do the thing that it believes is going to further to the uttermost Canada's war effort, all circumstances considered. May I say that when I say "all circumstances considered" I have in mind the conditions as they may exist in respect to the war in different theatres and the conditions that may exist in Canada itself.
We have heard on the floor of the house within the last few days suggestions made that we should send more men overseas to Britain. We have had other suggestions made that we should not send more men over to Britain but send men over to the Orient in larger numbers.

Who said:
"secret session"? My hon. friend may be giving away some facts which I can assure him, if he thinks they are secret, he should not give away. But what I am stating now has been said here in this parliament in open session since parliament opened. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) suggested that we should send an expedition to Australia. I have understood the hon. member who has just interrupted is in

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
favour of sending more men to Britain. We also have had suggested in this house in open session that we ought to be keeping our men here and not sending them across either the Atlantic or the Pacific. May I recall the words my hon. friend the leader of the opposition addressed to me when he was waxing eloquent over this matter? He said: With the enemy knocking at our very doors you are going to take this plebiscite. If the enemy is knocking at our very doors, I do not think there will be very much demand in this country to send men overseas. We shall in that eventuality be keeping all the men we can put at our very doors where they can do the most effective work. I believe myself that the most effective way to defeat the enemy is to defeat him away from our shores altogether so that he will never get near our shores. But I do say that if he ever comes battering on the shores of this country, public feeling in this country will be so strong that any government, no matter what its view might be, will -have to think twice before it adds to the number of men that are being sent out of Canada.
I mention these things because they help to illustrate how impossible it is for the government to give a decision here and now as to what it is going to do next September or October or November or December, or in 1943 or 1944. We cannot make any decision at the present time as to what we are going to do then, and we would be foolish if we led anyone to believe that we were going to be governed other than by all the facts that exist at the time this matter is under further consideration.
There is another matter. My hon. friend says that I ought to tell the people this and that. And yet he-perhaps not he, but several of those who sit around him hope that I shall not be here very long. The one thing they wish above everything else is that I should be out of office instead of in office.

speechtext:
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition ought to have a very kindly feeling towards myself on that particular question because he has seen efforts that have been made to have someone else take his place. They have not succeeded, and may I say to him sincerely that I think the country is much better off having him there to-day. I can tell him I am saying that not only on behalf of my own supporters but on behalf of a good many of his supporters as well. But I wish to make this clear. The present government, as I think my colleagues will bear me out, is not a one-man government. We are not imitating dictators; we are trying to remain the government of a democracy and to get as far away from dictatorship as we possibly can in all our actions. Any decision that is going to be made with respect to what will be done in a matter of future policy is not going to be made by any one menfber of the government or any two members; it is going to be made by all the members that sit in the government. Every member in the government will have his voice in the shaping of policy, and those who cannot accept the policy of the majority will find it convenient to retire, and a government will remain in office which will stand as one with respect to policy.
I could not if I wished, therefore, undertake to tell the people of Canada to-day what was going to be done some months hence by a government of which I might not be a member, or with respect to which different views might be entertained from those which I have, or which other of the present members of the administration may have. These facts are elementary. They should appeal to everyone who has to do with parliamentary procedure and government. Perhaps I can give an illustration that will help to make clear the wisdom of not indicating at the present time just what decision may be reached a little later on in certain circumstances.
In order to carry on war men are necessary, money is necessary. Both have to be raised, one in large numbers and the other in large quantities. With respect to the men that are being raised at the present time we have two methods. They are not ends in themselves but methods, and we are taking the method which we believe will be most effective and serviceable to Canada's war effort when we resort to the one or to the other. We have two methods of raising men for the army. Some of them are raised by compulsion; they are serving within the territorial limits of
832	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
Canada. Others are being raised by voluntary enlistment,'some of them also are serving in Canada. But all that are going overseas are being raised by the voluntary enlistment system, which has proved effective up to the present.
Now with respect to the raising of money, we are using the same two methods. We are raising money by compulsion, under taxation in its different forms; and we are raising money voluntarily by the loan system which is in progress at the present, time, and which the people of the country are supporting splendidly, and, I believe, will continue to support. Supposing my hon. friend were to ask me, "What are you going to do if the voluntary system fails in the matter of the loan? Will you tell the people that now?" Could I tell them that? Would it be wise to tell them that? But a decision will have to be made if the voluntary system in the matter of loans should fail to produce the results which it is necessary should be produced in the securing of an amount of money requisite for the purpose. Under such circumstances I think probably there would be resort to the conscription of wealth. I do not see any other alternative than for 'the government just to come along and take the wealth that exists, if the required sums cannot be raised voluntarily.

That might not be found sufficiently effective. However, I do not wish to be diverted from what I am saying because it is wholly pertinent. I wish to make it very clear, because through the next couple of weeks or months the people will be saying, "Why did not the Prime Minister state his position as to what he would do if this plebiscite did not carry or if it did carry?" I wish to have this parallel kept in mind. What the government is going to do when the voluntary method fails in the matter of loans it will decide when the time comes; and it will do exactly the same thing as respects the matter of raising men. When we find that we cannot raise the required numbers of men for enlistment overseas by the voluntary method, and it is absolutely necessary to raise more men by other methods, then we will make our decision, present it to parliament and have it discussed on its merits. I am putting this forward now so that the public may understand quite clearly why it is impossible to give any immediate decision. And may I say this: I think the 
people of the country will see to it that both things are linked pretty closely together if one or the other becomes necessary.
My hon. friend says we are asking that the government be given a blank cheque. What does he mean by a blank cheque? A blank cheque for what? Not a blank cheque to ignore parliament. The blank cheque is simply the cheque the government has with respect to all matters excepting this one thing, of the choice of method for raising men for overseas service. With respect to all other matters the government to-day has full power and authority. That may be the blank cheque If that is what he means by blank cheque, I say, let us have a complete blank cheque so that we can take whatever action we wish. But when he speaks of a blank cheque, what he is trying to infer is that the government is seeking to exercise some power independent of parliament. That is not what we are asking for in this plebiscite. We are simply asking to be given freedom to make an untrammelled decision and to come to parliament with that decision. Let my hon. friends keep that in mind, that before any measure can be passed in this parliament, no matter what it relates to, conscription or anything else, it has to get the support of a majority of the House of Commons, and the ministry has to consider very carefully every aspect of the question which will bear upon the situation in presenting any measure to parliament.
As to the conduct of the campaign, my hon. friend asked a word or two about that. I should hope that the campaign would be made an educational campaign which would help to impress upon the people the necessity of giving the government full power in time of war. I think it can be made that. My hon. friend and I are to-day agreed that the government ought to have this power and we are agreed for the same reason. And the leaders of the other parties are agreed. I know that the Social Credit party feels that something ought to be added, but at least I take it that they are not unwilling to give the government the freedom that is needed to act in such a way as will best serve the interests of the country. So that we are all pretty well agreed in this parliament that the government ought to have that power. But could we do anything better to serve the national interests of this country than, as representatives of all shades of opinion in this House of Commons, to go out to the people of Canada and tell them that this is a time when the war situation is so serious that no power should be withheld from the government in the administration of public affairs? I hope that course will be taken.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
My hon. friend asks me what the government's attitude on the plebiscite will be. 1 took care to state that at the time I was speaking on the address, and I should like to read this one word in conclusion, from page 51 of Hansard of January 26:
In the presentation of the plebiscite to the electorate the desire of the administration to possess complete freedom of action will of course, receive the vigorous and wholehearted support of all members of the government. It will, I hope receive the support of every member of parliament, and will, I believe, receive the support of the Canadian people.
There is nothing half-hearted about our purpose in this. I do not believe it will be possible for an administration to carry on, in a time like this, with the sense it ought to have of complete authority without being given complete power. It should not be put perpetually in a false position just because of some obligation necessary at an earlier time, but which, as I explained in the debate on the address, is having an effect quite different from that originally intended in its relation to the state of affairs that exists at the present moment. I have not gone into that this afternoon, because I spoke on it at length in the debate on the address. The reasons which to-day would actuate the people in respect of the powers being given to a government when we have war all over the world, on every continent and every ocean, are surely vastly different from what they were when we were contemplating a war which was expected, to be limited to the confines of Europe. I think that almost all the people realize that it is in their interest to give to the government, in time *of world-wide war the utmost powers that can possibly be given, realizing of course, that these powers can only be exercised in the light of its responsibility to parliament and that the government must receive the support of the majority in parliament before any measures can be given effect to.
