speechtext:
In regard to that I have this feeling. The people themselves will realize that the government would not ask for this full power unless it was in the interest of the people themselves that it should be given to the government. This matter is one that affects their lives. The situation is different from a general election; it is not a general election to decide between one party and another, but it is a matter that affects
the home of every individual, that may affect the life of every individual in the country, certainly will affect the future of every individual, and will determine to what extent every man, woman and child in this country is to be half slave and half free or wholly slave or wholly free. If the people understand that and if hon. members will present the case to their constituents, pointing out the seriousness of the war and the state of the world at the present time and how it is to the people's own interests that they give the government full power, I think the people will come out and vote.
Also there is no reason why voluntary organizations should not be furthered to the utmost. Those who feel deeply-and I think that includes most of the people in this country-should organize themselves into voluntary groups to bring the people out. Let me make this perfectly clear so that there can be no mistake about it; if the vote should be overwhelmingly in support of the question asked in the plebiscite I shall not for one moment claim that it is a vote of confidence in this particular government in the carrying on of the war, but that it is a vote by the people of this country to give to any government the right to have and to feel it has the full power and authority which a government should have under conditions such as exist at this time of war.
Let me make this very clear, because it has been said that the government will claim a large majority as a great victory for itself, we are past the time when anyone can afford to talk in terms of party politics. We have in the recent by-elections had one illustration of the folly and baneful effect of doing that sort of thing through the amount of controversy to which they gave rise. Let us seek to unite ourselves, and here is the ground on which we can be united, to tell the people the situation, a situation so serious that they must show to the country at large that they are prepared to give to the government all the possible power needed to deal with it.
One other point. A great deal has been said in different parts of the world, and in our own country, about the New Order that is to come when this war is over. I have said on two or three occasions, I feel it very deeply, that unless that new order emerges and asserts itself before the war is over we shall see very little of any new order when the war is over.
What is the old order that is to give place to something new? The old order, the order which has brought on this war, is an order which attaches no value whatever to any treaty, to any contract, to any pledge, to any obligation, to anything that is honourable, but which says that no matter how deceitful, how

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
crooked, how wrong, whatever will get results through might and force, is the order that should be followed in the world. In other words, its supporters seek to build a totalitarian world on deceit, and betrayal, doing away with free institutions, doing away with democratic government, doing away altogether with any real relationship between the people and their governing institutions. Does anyone in this assembly believe that Hitler would ever have been permitted or able to go to war if a free parliament had been maintained in Germany? Does anyone believe that Mussolini if he had not worked into the position that he did of complete control himself over his people and above them would ever have had the freedom to bring that country into the war? The thing the people are going to demand in the new order is that all relationships, so far as it is possible to have them so, between a government and a people shall be maintained on the highest grounds on which they oan be maintained. They will insist on public honour in the transaction of public business, and they will insist above everything else that the government that is carrying on the affairs of their country shall be responsive to the will of the people and see that it is administering that will and no other.
A good deal has been said about leadership and lack of leadership. The question of individual leadership is a small matter, men come and men go and they are soon forgotten. But the history of nations continues to be remembered through generations. Canada has taken a great place in this war. Canada's war effort, I believe, is something that when the war is over and we get through with political controversy the people of this country will be more proud of than any other thing in the history of this Dominion; because it has been, in Mr. Churchill's own words, a magnificent effort and all of us should seek to have it known as such. And as I have said over and over again, it is not the effort of the government, it is the effort of the people of Canada. What the government has been able to do has been done only by virtue of what the people have been prepared to allow them to do. In connection with the new order of things which is to control the future, I say that this country apart from its war effort in the aspects we have been discussing here has in some other particulars set a noble example to every nation. And they are particulars which relate to the future of democracy, and to the question of whether democracy is possible or not. We were told that it was not possible for a people to decide in their own free parliament whether they should go to war or not; that that decision had to be made for them by some government before they were assembled together. Well, this country has proved the 
opposite, Canada has shown the world that the representatives of the people brought together from all parts of the dominion in a free parliament are able to decide, and to decide promptly the position which they will take with regard to participation in war. That is a great gain for democracy.
Another thing which Canada has done has been to show the world that it is possible for a democracy to see that the people's voice continues to govern in its affairs even in a time of war; that those clauses in its constitution which have been framed for the purpose of preserving the rights of the people in their own affairs of government can be exercised in times of war as well as in times of peace. Some of us were told that we could not have an election in war time, that it was all wrong, would create confusion and the like. Well, the government did not view it in that way, the people of Canada did not view it in that way. We had our election in war time; and we are able to say, as Lincoln said at the time of the civil war, "The whole purpose of the people's concern in the war itself would have been lost, if the people had to be deprived of the fundamental rights which were reserved to them by their constitution." We have not usurped the constitution of this country. We have held to it; and I view with a good deal of concern this business of assemblies perpetuating their own existence for indefinite periods of time without allowing the people to have any voice in the matter, regardless of what their constitution may be. I think the people are able to look after themselves in these matters if they are given an opportunity to do so.	.
There are two outstanding achievements, in the nature of a national example. I put third, although perhaps most important of all, that the government of a country should have a sense of its moral obligations as well as a sense of its legal obligations. There has been very little said in the Tecent past about moral obligations on the part of nations, but unless I am greatly mistaken there is nothing that is going to mean as much in the future of mankind. If we are going to rule out of our public life the honour of public men and of parliament; if we are going to rule out those things which above all else we have been taught all our lives to regard as most sacred, namely the promise, the word that is better than the bond, the contract expressed or implied that has been made between a government and its people, the treaties between nations-if these things are to be ruled out of our public life then public life will become chaos indeed. But if we allow the people to

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Diejenbaker
see that when we do give a pledge, when we do assume power at their instance, we are continually reminded of the source from which that power comes; that we are going to honour their rights as we seek to honour our own conscience, so we shall be laying the foundation of the kind of order that will be enduring through the years to come.

Naturally, Mr. Speaker, I cannot begin to follow the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in all the arguments that he has advanced. As I listened to the termination of his speech and the plea for a new order. I could not but agree with his words. If only that plea had been made in the beginning of his address, for a new order in Canada at this time, a new order free from political partisanship and with only one thing in mind -the desire to be guided in what we do by the opportunity and the challenge that is ours -it would have been something to inspire this country at this time.
The Prime Minister says, "Trust the people." Yet, Mr. Speaker, does he trust the people when he fails to place before them the question they will be required to answer? They are not told what is going to happen after this question is answered. I thought, as the right hon. gentleman spoke, that he would have told the people of Canada, in language that would be unmistakable, of the challenge to this country at this time; of the need for action; of the necessity, if you will, that he be relieved of his responsibilities incident to this commitment, and of what he would do, and the leadership he would give, if Canada should release him from that commitment. Five or six weeks have gone by in this session; the question has been asked over and over again of the government and the Prime Minister: What are you going to do? That is what the people of Canada want to know to-day.
You have been told.
The hon. gentleman says we have been told.
Of course you have.
In one province we have been told that there will be nothing done; in other parts of Canada we have been told that selective service will be brought into effect. We do not know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend says the people have been told these things. Will he tell us by what authoritative source that has been said? Will he cite one case of anyone with any authority to speak in the matter who has made any such statement?
44561-53J

Well, Mr. Speaker, the by-election campaigns just concluded were characterized in one province by the stand taken by the premier of that province that no action is contemplated, which was clear and unequivocal, and in other parts of Canada the stand taken was that there would be action. Yet to-day, when events are taking place the like of which this empire has never seen; with Java being attacked, with the Malay states overrun and with Singapore fallen, the Prime Minister of Canada says things are not yet serious enough to demand further action in the matter of man-power. Singapore, it is said, fell partly because of the lack of man-power. But the answer by the Prime Minister as to what action will be taken is that he cannot tell the people at this time and that it will remain his secret, a secret that time and circumstance alone may reveal.
I have in my hand a copy of the bill. Why does it not incorporate the question to be asked of the people? This bill as placed before parliament will have but one result. It will change the constitutional history of this dominion, in that it will permit the Prime Minister at any time from this day on to submit a plebiscite on any matter whatsoever to the people of Canada, with the authority of this parliament. It is so worded, Mr. Speaker, that it is operative beyond the war. It is so worded that the Prime Minister can continue to submit plebiscites at any time and without restriction. Let me ask this question. Why was not the method followed this time similar to that adopted in submitting the plebiscite of 1898? In my opinion this bill represents a milestone along the way that will destroy responsible government. The Prime Minister has said in effect that a great harm was done to the principle of responsible government in 1940 when he promised that there would never be conscription for overseas service, and. now in effect wishes to undo the harm so that responsible government may be restored again.
I am not dealing to-day with the arguments that have been advanced against the taking of a plebiscite containing these words: "Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligations arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for overseas service?" I repeat, and this epitomizes my viewpoint on this subject, that the submission of this plebiscite in those words without the people of Canada knowing in advance what the government intends to do, or without even a suggestion as to what the government intends to do, is going to divide the people of this country as never before; that it is the repudiation of governmental

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Diejenbaker
responsibility, and just one more step along the road that leads to derision o-f parliament and of parliamentary institutions generally.
The Prime Minister for years-in fact during all his political life-has stood for the principle of the supremacy of parliament, and he has stressed that position since 1935. But what is the record? This legislation falls in line with his attitude toward parliament since 1935. I realize that during war time there is a necessity for orders in council incident to the carrying on of the war, but that does not excuse the issuing of orders in council in ever-increasing manner with respect to peacetime measures as well. There is no justification for that at all.
Only yesterday it was revealed that since the outbreak of war 20,677 orders in council had been issued, and that of that number 5,470 had been passed while parliament was in session. Yes, even since parliament has been in session in the last five weeks 412 orders in. council have been passed. So general has this situation become that when I asked a question in the house as to how many statutes of parliament had been changed or suspended by orders in council the Prime Minister of Canada could give me no particulars. He said in effect that there were too many of them, and that it would be difficult if not impossible to give the information. The answer he made on May 19, 1941, is reported at page 2912 of Hansard, in reply to the question whether any orders in council purporting to change or suspend the operation of the provisions of any dominion statute, either in whole or in part, had been passed since the outbreak of war. He said:
I might reply orally to this question. To the first part the answer is yes.
Then the Prime Minister continued:
As to the second-
A question, by the way, which asked for details-and surely the people of Canada have a right to know what statutes passed by parliament have been suspended or amended by order in council-
-I am informed by the clerk of the council that there is no separate index of orders in council which amend statutes, and that it would require a great deal of research to discover the different orders which might have that effect and also to reply to the question as to the operative effect of the respective orders so passed.
That answer means that while this parliament is supreme, the government is unable to tell what statutes have been amended or suspended by order in council.	*
What of the supremacy of parliament now? Almost every day, regulations with all the force of law are passed by the governor in

council, by ministers of the crown, by heads of departments and by government agencies and boards, until we have reached the position where seventy-five per cent, if not more, of the laws put into effect since the war began1, and which affect the lives of every citizen in Canada, have been passed not by this parliament but by this indirect method. Parliament is constantly receding in importance as the trend continues unabated.
We have before us in this bill the latest step. This measure was drafted by exceptionally able legal draftsmen, and in my opinion the omissions are not unintentional.
I am not now opposing the plebiscite to release the government from its pledge. I am not here for the purpose of adopting an attitude of obstruction and I may point out that while this parliament has been in session for more than five weeks at the most serious time in the history of the British empire, any delays w'hich have arisen have not been caused by the official opposition. Less than one-fifth of the time in debate has been taken up by us. We placed our views before parliament, in opposition to the submission of this plebiscite, but the majority in this house have decided that a plebiscite should be submitted to the people of Canada, and we must abide by that decision. A plebiscite is to be taken regardless of the fact that in the long history of Great Britain, with all the constitutional changes which have taken place, no government has ever submitted any matter to the people by way of plebiscite. In Canada such procedure is a departure, excepting, as was mentioned by the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), in the case of the liquor plebiscite submitted to the people in 1898.
To illustrate the difference I should point out that under the measure as it now appears before parliament the Prime Minister and his government do not have to submit any questions to the people, whereas under the plebiscite of 1898 the question to be asked was in the statute. The other major difference is that the government may submit as many questions as they choose when they choose. They may place a plebiscite on any question before the people at any time in the future. There is no control whatsoever-and I intend to refer to those sections which have particular reference to that situation. The statute of 1898 allowed for only one submission. Mr. Speaker, while the empire fights, Canada plebiscites.
When the statute was passed in 1898 there was nothing evasive in the attitude of the government. The question was put in the statute. The regulations as to voting were contained in the statute. The elections act,

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Diefenbaker
with the necessary changes, was incorporated in that statute. The act is chapter 51 of the statutes for 1898. Section 3 is as follows:
There shall he submitted to vote of electors hereinafter declared entitled to vote thereon the following question:
_ Are you in favour of am act prohibiting the importation and manufacture or sale of spirits, wine, ale, beer, eider and all other alcoholic liquors for use as beverages?
It even states how the ballot paper is to be worded, and what question is to be placed on it.
What about the measure now before us? If I am correct-and I believe anyone reading the bill will conclude that I am-this bill is plebiscite legislation, and by the authority of this parliament if passed it will establish in Canada the right to govern by way of plebiscite. Unless the bill is restricted in its scope, from now on the government of Canada may continue to submit questions, without any control whatsoever.
The Prime Minister has spoken about responsible government. Is it not the principle of responsible government that the elected representatives of the people shall legislate for the safety and welfare of the state, and that the government shall continue in office so long as it has the support of the majority in parliament? When that support is lost, an election follows where no person or group can command the support of the majority.
As I listened to the Prime Minister terminate his remarks to-day I wondered whether they were not in fact a prelude to an election regardless of the outcome of the plebiscite. His speech indicated that possibility to me. Here is the bill as it has been submitted to this house, and I am going to refer to it in some detail. Section 1 reads:
This act may be cited as the Dominion Plebiscite Act, 1942.
That is general enough. Then the bill goes on to define the various persons who are entitled to vote, and it defines plebiscite as follows:
(d) "plebiscite" or "dominion plebiscite" means the taking of a vote on the question set out in a proclamation of the governor in council issued under section three of this act.
If the Prime Minister, under section 3 of the bill, had set out the question to be asked, then there would be no doubt that this bill contemplated only one plebiscite for a definite purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but may I say that I did make it quite clear to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) when he referred to the same matter that I could see no reason whatever why the question itself
should not be inserted in the bill. I hope it will be by the committee.
Why not make this a special bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is all it was intended to be.

Apparently the Prime Minister did not get his ideas across to the draftsman of the bill. If this bill becomes law, if it is passed in its present form, we are going to have in Canada government by plebiscite, not by responsible government.
The insertion of the particular question would avoid any possibility of that.

But this is the bill upon which we are asked to vote. If we pass this bill we allow the government to submit a plebiscite at its will, at any time and on any matter whatsoever, and against that I protest. Let me read section 3:
3.	(1) The governor in council may by proclamation order the taking of a plebiscite under the provisions of this act.
(2) The proclamation shall state fully the question to be submitted to the voters at the plebiscite in the same words and form as it will appear on the ballot papers to be used at the plebiscite.
It becomes perfectly clear that unless the members of this house, representing as we do the people of Canada, demand that the question to be asked be embodied ini the bill, we are giving to the government, not a blank cheque but the right to submit any matter they choose to the people of Canada at any time. There is nowhere any limitation on so doing. Section 5 reads:
Any person who shall have voted at a plebiscite taken under the provisions of this act during the present war shall thereafter be ineligible-
"During the present war." Why the insertion of the provision that these people shall be ineligible when they have voted at a plebiscite during the present war if only one plebiscite is to be submitted? These significant words reveal the situation exactly. The statute will continue in effect beyond the termination of this war, but the only disqualification of exemption from military service of conscientious objectors would be in connection with anyone who had voted during the period of the war. This shows the danger of legislation such as this unless it is strictly limited within the ambit of the question that the Prime Minister says will be submitted to the people of Canada.
The leader of the opposition gave the government warning on Friday last of what our attitude would be in this regard and of

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Diejenbaker
our wish to have the question included in the bill, but it has persisted in placing this bill before parliament in this form. Therefore, we feel that we have the duty to move an amendment to ensure the inclusion of the question in clear and unmistakable language.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth):
That the bill be not now read a. second time but that this house is of the opinion that the use of the powers conferred thereby be restricted to the submission thereunder of one plebiscite only.
I intend now to make a few suggestions with regard to the bill. I repeat that I think the government should have told the country what it is going to do after the vote has been taken. To-day it is Janus-faced; in one part of Canada it looks one way, in another part it looks another way. The Prime Minister says that he thinks the people will give an all-out vote. I hope they do, because there would be nothing more tragic if this plebiscite were defeated. We on this side of the house have asked the Prime Minister to tell the people of Canada just how serious he regards the situation, but without avail and the only conclusion that can be taken from the speech of the Prime Minister is that conditions are not serious, for he has stated clearly that he would not think of asking for more man-power under the selective system as conditions are at this time.
I should like to see a one hundred per cent vote on this matter. I do not believe in a compulsory system of getting out votes, but I do ask the Prime Minister and the government to shake themselves out of the lethargy they are in and tell the people of the gravity of the empire's position and of the imperative need of action. Many people are going to fail to vote because they believe that this is a vote of confidence in the government. The Prime Minister has said that he would not interpret a favourable vote as a vote of confidence. I do not care how it is interpreted. Time is running against us and he should act. "Wait and see" is apparently to be the policy of this government, even to-day as we listened to the casualties in Hong Kong.
I repeat that the people have a right to know at this time what the government intends to do. I am not one to advocate a sit-down strike as far as voting on this matter is concerned for such action would be reprehensible. The government asks us over here to be Willkies, but I ask the Prime Minister to be a Roosevelt from now on, and to refer to the war effort of this nation not as the governments' war effort but as the war effort of Canada.
You did hear him say that, my friend.

That was after he
had referred several times with exultation to the results of the campaign that recently took place. In the last paragraph of his address he did ask the Canadian people to regard this as a Canadian war effort. Why wait ten weeks for a vote on this matter? The ordinary routine peace-time election procedure should [DOT] not apply to-day. We should shorten up that period. Where shall we be in ten weeks? Only on Thursday last we read in the press that if Java falls and Australia be attacked., the next places on the Japanese time-table to be attacked are Hawaii and Alaska in April.
Voluntary workers should be asked for over the radio. Why were not great patriotic organizations in this country asked to take over this work? But they will not do it enthusiastically, Mr. Speaker, unless they know that in getting out and working to the end that this government may be empowered to do something, the government, when it gets the power is actually going to act and without delay.
I have had complaint after complaint over the suggestion that men are going to be sent overseas for the purpose of taking the vote. In my opinion such a course is unnecessary. Send the ballots over to Canadian general headquarters in Great Britain, have them distributed to the divisions and battalions, and set out in military orders the date of the voting, have the voting take place at battalion headquarters. What does the government intend to do in regard to the counting of the soldiers' votes?
I commend the government and am glad that it has stood firm against those who would have had all the votes in Canada thrown into one common container. That would have done away with initiative in every province and every constituency of this dominion. I commend the Prime Minister for the course he has adopted of letting each province and each constituency know just how it stands on this question.
But so far as the voting overseas is concerned I do think this, that the men who to-day are serving this country know what they want, and' I would not divide their votes among the constituencies. I suggest that their votes be counted without regard to constituency so that we can have the message of the men overseas in a united voice as to what they think the government should be doing at this time.
I have nothing more to say, Mr. Speaker, except again to point out the necessity of having the bill as it now stands amended at once as I have suggested, and with that in mind I have moved an amendment. To do otherwise would be for us to pass another milestone in this dominion beyond the point we have

Questions
reached to-day in the decline of responsible government. Parliament is being emasculated *as a result of the creation of administrative boards of all kinds and order in council government. This act unless amended may well be just another milestone towards the destruction of that which we are fighting to preserve in these days of war-our free parliamentary institutions characterized by the principle of responsible government*

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I raise a point of older, Mr. Speaker. I submit that the amendment is out of order, and I raise the point now in order that your honour may have an opportunity to consider the matter. The amendment tends to amend the bill, which I do not think is right, and the amendment does not Object to the principle of the bill.
On motion of Mr. Veniot the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 5.55 pm.
